en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Ten Birth Stories,
Chapter on the Four Gates.
12. The Birth Story of the Cat and the Cock “Even those who do not eat desire to obtain food when it is found; how much more so for those who are virtuous!”
What is it that you cook for yourself which you do not give away? That is not right.
It is through stinginess and negligence.
Thus, a gift is not given;
by one who desires merit and understands, it ought to be given.
The very thing that the miser fears and does not give,
that same thing becomes a source of fear for him when he does not possess it: hunger and thirst.
The miser fears that very thing which touches him,
both in this world and in the next— the fool himself.
Therefore, having overcome stinginess and conquered impurity,
one should give gifts;
for merits follow one in the world beyond.
They become a refuge for living beings.
For those who give what is hard to give,
performing deeds that are difficult to perform;
The wicked do not act in accordance with the virtuous;
the way of the good is difficult to follow.
Therefore, [one should distinguish] between the virtuous and the wicked.
Diverse are the destinations from here:
the wicked go to hell,
while the virtuous are destined for heaven.
Some give away little,
while others do not wish to give much;
yet an offering given from even a little [is of great merit].
“Measured by a thousand [pieces of gold],” [it is said].
“One should practice the Dhamma even if one lives as a scavenger,
supporting a wife and children on meager means.”
"A thousand times a hundred thousand sacrifices of a thousand-sacrificer do not equal even a fraction of such a one as you.
"For what reason is this sacrifice so vast and of great value?"
The gift given with equanimity is beyond price;
even ten thousand times ten thousand sacrifices performed by those who give thousands cannot equal even a fraction of such a gift as yours.
“Some, established in what is uneven,
give after cutting, killing, and then causing grief;
that gift is tearful and accompanied by punishment.”
The gift given with equanimity is not worth even a fraction of that which is given by one such as you, who has performed a thousand sacrifices of hundreds of thousands.
The Twelfth Jātaka: The Story of the Cat and the Cock.
